lessons.title: Understanding Guinea Fowl and Quail Laying Cycles
lessons.body: Guinea fowl and quail have different laying cycles. Guinea fowl hens start laying at 28-32 weeks (7-8 months) and produce 80-150 eggs per year, mostly between March and October in Africa. They lay in the afternoon, often in hidden nests. Quail start laying at 6-8 weeks and can produce 250-300 eggs per year if well managed. They lay in the late afternoon or early evening. In Africa, quail lay best when temperatures are between 18-24Â°C; above 30Â°C, production drops. Guinea fowl are seasonal breeders, triggered by longer daylight. In West Africa, peak laying is during the rainy season (May-September). To check if a hen is laying, look at her vent: it should be moist, wide, and pink. For quail, check the vent for dryness and size. Keep records: write down daily egg numbers per pen. A simple notebook works. For guinea fowl, provide dark, quiet nests with straw. For quail, use small boxes with soft bedding. Collect eggs daily to prevent breakage and eating. In Africa, many farmers lose eggs to snakes, rats, and other predators. Use raised cages for quail and secure houses for guinea fowl. If you want chicks, keep a ratio of 1 male to 4-5 females for guinea fowl, and 1 male to 3 females for quail. Too many males cause stress and lower egg production. Replace breeding stock every 2 years for guinea fowl and every year for quail. With proper care, your birds will lay consistently and give you good income.

lessons.title: Collecting and Storing Eggs for Sale or Hatching
lessons.body: Collect eggs at least twice a day, early morning and late afternoon. For guinea fowl, check hidden nests in bushes; they often lay on the ground. For quail, collect from the cage floor or roll-out trays. Use clean hands or a soft cloth. Never use water to wash eggs unless very dirty; if you must, use warm water (32-35Â°C) with a little bleach (1 teaspoon per litre) and dry immediately. For sale, store eggs in a cool, dark place at 15-20Â°C. In hot African climates, use a clay pot with wet sand or a cooler box with ice packs. Eggs for hatching should be stored at 15-18Â°C and 75% humidity for no more than 7 days. Turn them twice daily. For guinea fowl, store eggs pointed end down in egg trays. For quail, use small trays with holes. Never store eggs near strong smells like onions or kerosene; they absorb odours. For sale, grade by size: small, medium, large. Guinea fowl eggs are small (35-45g) and brown with speckles; quail eggs are 8-12g and speckled. Pack in clean cartons or trays. For hatching, select only clean, uncracked, normal-shaped eggs. Discard double-yolk or tiny eggs. In Africa, many farmers sell eggs to local markets, hotels, and restaurants. Build relationships with buyers. Keep records of collection dates and storage conditions. If you plan to hatch, use an incubator or a broody hen. Guinea fowl eggs hatch in 26-28 days; quail in 17-18 days. Always collect eggs before they get dirty or broken.

lessons.title: Improving Egg Production Through Lighting and Nutrition
lessons.body: Light and feed are the two biggest factors for egg production. Guinea fowl need 14-16 hours of light per day to lay well. In Africa, natural daylight varies. If you want eggs in the dry season, use a solar-powered LED bulb or a kerosene lamp (careful with fire) for 2-3 hours before sunrise or after sunset. For quail, provide 14-16 hours of light; a 40-watt bulb in a 3x3m room is enough. Keep lights on a timer to avoid stress. Nutrition: layers need 16-18% protein. Mix your own feed: 40% maize, 20% soybean meal, 15% fish meal, 10% wheat bran, 10% sunflower cake, 5% limestone or oyster shell. Add vitamin premix (2g per kg feed). For guinea fowl, also provide green leaves like kale or amaranth. For quail, use a commercial layer mash or make a crumble. Always provide clean water. Add electrolytes or vitamins during heat stress. In Africa, many farmers use kitchen scraps; avoid oily or salty foods. Give crushed oyster shell free-choice for strong eggshells. A good layer eats 100-120g feed per day (guinea fowl) or 25-30g (quail). Collect eggs daily; frequent collection encourages more laying. Keep stress low: avoid loud noises, predators, and overcrowding. Guinea fowl need 2-3 square feet per bird; quail need 0.5-1 square foot. With proper lighting and feed, you can get 70-80% production from quail and 40-50% from guinea fowl. In hot weather, feed early morning and evening. Keep records of feed and egg numbers to see what works.

lessons.title: Egg Quality: Cleaning, Grading, and Packaging
lessons.body: Egg quality affects price and customer trust. Never wash eggs unless necessary; the natural bloom protects against bacteria. If dirty, wipe with a dry cloth or fine sandpaper. For stubborn dirt, use warm water with a little vinegar (1 tablespoon per litre) and dry immediately. Do not soak. Grade eggs by size and shell condition. For guinea fowl: small (under 35g), medium (35-40g), large (over 40g). For quail: small (under 8g), medium (8-10g), large (over 10g). Remove cracked, misshapen, or very dirty eggs; sell them cheaply for immediate use or discard. For hatching, only use clean, normal-shaped eggs. Packaging: use clean egg trays or cartons. For guinea fowl, standard 30-egg trays. For quail, 30-egg trays with small holes or 12-egg cartons. Label with date and grade. In Africa, many markets sell eggs in plastic bags or loose; using proper packaging reduces breakage and increases value. For transport, pack eggs in crates with straw or paper between layers. Keep out of direct sun. For sale to hotels, use branded cartons. Store eggs in a cool place; if you have a fridge, keep at 10-15Â°C. For hatching, store at 15-18Â°C and turn daily. Clean and disinfect trays after each use. Train workers to handle eggs gently. A simple grading table: size, weight, shell condition, and price. Set prices: large eggs cost more. In many African countries, quail eggs sell for 2-3 times more than chicken eggs per unit. Build a reputation for quality; customers will return.

lessons.title: Calculating Cost per Egg and Setting Your Selling Price
lessons.body: To make a profit, you must know your cost per egg. Start by calculating feed cost: a guinea fowl eats 110g/day, and feed costs $0.40/kg, so $0.044/day. Quail eats 30g/day, so $0.012/day. Add other costs: labour, housing, medication, water, and lighting. Suppose you have 100 guinea fowl hens: feed cost $4.40/day. Labour $2/day, medication $0.50/day, lighting $0.30/day, total $7.20/day. If they lay 50 eggs/day, cost per egg = $7.20/50 = $0.144. For 100 quail: feed $1.20/day, labour $1/day, medication $0.20/day, lighting $0.20/day, total $2.60/day. If they lay 70 eggs/day, cost per egg = $2.60/70 = $0.037. Now add a profit margin. In Africa, guinea fowl eggs sell for $0.20-0.30 each; quail eggs for $0.10-0.15 each. If your cost is $0.144, selling at $0.25 gives $0.106 profit per egg. For quail, cost $0.037, sell at $0.12 gives $0.083 profit. But check local market prices. Sell in bulk to restaurants for a lower price but guaranteed sales. Sell retail at markets for higher price. Keep records of all expenses and income. Adjust feed if costs rise. Use local ingredients to lower feed cost. For example, grow your own maize or buy in bulk. Also consider egg size: large eggs cost more to produce but sell higher. Calculate cost per egg every month. If cost is too high, find ways to reduce: use solar lighting, make your own feed, reduce labour. Set price at least 20% above cost. But don't overprice; check competitors. A simple formula: Selling price = Cost per egg + (Cost per egg x 0.3). For guinea fowl: $0.144 + $0.043 = $0.187, round to $0.20. For quail: $0.037 + $0.011 = $0.048, round to $0.05, but market may pay more. Always aim for profit.

lessons.title: Dealing with Egg-Bound Hens and Other Laying Issues
lessons.body: Egg-bound hens cannot pass an egg. Signs: straining, sitting, tail pumping, swollen abdomen. It is common in quail and guinea fowl, especially if they lack calcium or are overweight. To treat, first isolate the hen in a warm, dark place. Give a warm bath (not hot) for 10-15 minutes to relax muscles. Apply a little vegetable oil to the vent with a clean finger. Gently massage the abdomen. If the egg is visible, you can try to remove it with oiled fingers, but be careful not to break it. If broken, flush with warm water and consult a vet. Prevent egg-binding by providing free-choice oyster shell or crushed limestone. Ensure feed has 3-4% calcium. For quail, add 2% calcium. Avoid feeding too much energy feed. Keep birds active. Other laying issues: soft-shelled eggs (lack of calcium or vitamin D3), double-yolk eggs (normal in young hens), and egg eating (boredom or lack of protein). To stop egg eating, collect eggs frequently, provide dark nests, and add fake eggs or golf balls. For prolapse, keep the hen clean and isolate; apply honey or petroleum jelly. In Africa, many farmers lose hens to egg-binding because they don't notice early. Check your birds daily. If a hen is frequently egg-bound, cull her. Also, watch for mites and lice, which cause stress and lower production. Dust with wood ash or diatomaceous earth. Provide clean water and good ventilation. For guinea fowl, keep nests low to the ground. For quail, use roll-away trays to prevent egg eating. Record any health issues and treat quickly. A healthy hen lays well. If you see a drop in production, check feed, water, light, and parasites. Simple interventions save lives and money.

quiz.q: At what age do guinea fowl hens typically start laying?
quiz.explanation: Guinea fowl hens start laying at 28-32 weeks (7-8 months) of age.

quiz.q: How many eggs per year can a well-managed quail produce?
quiz.explanation: Quail can produce 250-300 eggs per year under good management.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for quail egg production?
quiz.explanation: Quail lay best when temperatures are between 18-24Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a guinea fowl hen is laying?
quiz.explanation: A laying hen has a moist, wide, and pink vent.

quiz.q: How often should you collect eggs from guinea fowl and quail?
quiz.explanation: Collect eggs at least twice a day to prevent breakage and eating.

quiz.q: What is the correct male-to-female ratio for guinea fowl breeding?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1 male to 4-5 females is recommended for guinea fowl.

quiz.q: How should you store eggs for hatching?
quiz.explanation: Hatching eggs should be stored at 15-18Â°C and 75% humidity for no more than 7 days.

quiz.q: What should you do if eggs are dirty before storage?
options: B) Wipe with a dry cloth
quiz.explanation: Wipe with a dry cloth or fine sandpaper; avoid washing unless necessary.

quiz.q: How long can guinea fowl hatching eggs be stored?
quiz.explanation: Store for no more than 7 days for best hatchability.

quiz.q: What is the weight range for a large guinea fowl egg?
quiz.explanation: Large guinea fowl eggs are over 40g.

quiz.q: How many hours of light per day do guinea fowl need for good egg production?
quiz.explanation: Guinea fowl need 14-16 hours of light per day to lay well.

quiz.q: What protein percentage should layer feed have?
quiz.explanation: Layers need 16-18% protein for good egg production.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good calcium source for laying birds?
quiz.explanation: Oyster shell or limestone provides calcium for strong eggshells.

quiz.q: How much feed does a guinea fowl layer eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A guinea fowl layer eats 100-120g of feed per day.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of soft-shelled eggs?
quiz.explanation: Soft-shelled eggs are often caused by a lack of calcium or vitamin D3.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid washing eggs?
options: B) It removes the natural bloom
quiz.explanation: Washing removes the natural bloom that protects against bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store eggs for sale in hot climates?
options: B) In a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Store eggs in a cool, dark place at 15-20Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a sign of an egg-bound hen?
options: D) Laying two eggs a day
quiz.explanation: Straining, sitting, and tail pumping are signs of egg-binding.

quiz.q: How can you prevent egg-binding?
quiz.explanation: Free-choice oyster shell or limestone provides calcium to prevent egg-binding.

quiz.q: What should you do first if a hen is egg-bound?
quiz.explanation: A warm bath helps relax muscles and may help pass the egg.

quiz.q: How do you calculate cost per egg?
options: A) Total daily costs divided by number of eggs
B) Number of eggs divided by feed cost
quiz.explanation: Cost per egg = total daily costs (feed, labour, etc.) divided by number of eggs collected.

quiz.q: If daily costs are $7.20 and you collect 50 eggs, what is the cost per egg?
What is a recommended profit margin above cost?
quiz.explanation: Set price at least 20-30% above cost per egg.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of feed and egg numbers?
options: A) To calculate cost per egg
quiz.explanation: Records help you calculate cost per egg and adjust management.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of egg eating in quail?
options: B) Boredom or lack of protein
quiz.explanation: Egg eating can be caused by boredom or a lack of protein.

quiz.q: How can you stop egg eating?
quiz.explanation: Frequent collection, dark nests, and fake eggs all help stop egg eating.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a double-yolk egg?
quiz.explanation: Double-yolk eggs are usually very large and normal in young hens.

quiz.q: How often should you replace breeding quail?
quiz.explanation: Replace breeding quail every year for best production.

quiz.q: What is the incubation period for quail eggs?
quiz.explanation: Quail eggs hatch in 17-18 days.

quiz.q: What is the incubation period for guinea fowl eggs?
quiz.explanation: Guinea fowl eggs hatch in 26-28 days.
